lessons.title: Least Common Multiple
lessons.objective: I can find the least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers by listing or comparing their multiples.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain how I found the LCM using the words multiple, common multiple, skip counting, and least common multiple.

concept.heading: What is the least common multiple (LCM)?
concept.intro: A multiple is what you get when you count by a number: 4, 8, 12, 16. The least common multiple is the smallest multiple that two numbers share.
concept.keyIdea: Least Common Multiple (LCM). 1. Skip count multiples of each number starting with the larger number. 2. Identify the first non-zero multiple that appears in both lists. 3. Prime factorization method: Product of highest powers of all prime factors

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I want the LCM of 4 and 6. I skip count the multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.
Then I skip count the multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24.
I look for the first number in BOTH lists. 12 is in both lists, and it comes before 24.
So the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. I check: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so both go into 12 evenly.
linesEs: Quiero el mínimo común múltiplo de 4 y 6. Cuento de salto los múltiplos de 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.
Luego cuento de salto los múltiplos de 6: 6, 12, 18, 24.
Busco el primer número que esté en las dos listas. El 12 está en las dos, y viene antes que el 24.
Entonces el mínimo común múltiplo de 4 y 6 es 12. Lo compruebo: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 y 12 ÷ 6 = 2, así que los dos caben exactamente en 12.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's find the LCM of 3 and 5. What are the multiples of 3? (3, 6, 9, 12, 15.)
What are the multiples of 5? (5, 10, 15.) What is the first number in both lists? (15.)
So the LCM of 3 and 5 is 15.
linesEs: Hallemos el mínimo común múltiplo de 3 y 5. ¿Cuáles son los múltiplos de 3? (3, 6, 9, 12, 15.)
¿Cuáles son los múltiplos de 5? (5, 10, 15.) ¿Cuál es el primer número que está en las dos listas? (15.)
Entonces el mínimo común múltiplo de 3 y 5 es 15.

vocabulary.definition: The least positive number that is a multiple of two or more numbers.
vocabulary.example: Multiples of 4 and 6 first meet at 12, so LCM = 12.

vocabulary.definition: What you get when you multiply a number by 1, 2, 3, and so on.
A number that two or more numbers both go into.
vocabulary.example: 12, 24, and 36 are all common multiples of both 3 and 4

vocabulary.definition: Counting by a number, like 2, 4, 6, to list its multiples.
vocabulary.example: Skip count by 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 — each jump adds 6

vocabulary.definition: Writing a number as prime numbers multiplied together. It helps you find the LCM.
vocabulary.example: 4 = 2 × 2, 6 = 2 × 3. LCM uses the highest power of each prime: 2² × 3 = 12

lessons.title: Prime Factorization
lessons.objective: I can write a number as a product of its prime factors using a factor tree.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain how I broke a number down using the words prime number, composite number, factor, and exponent.

concept.heading: What is prime factorization?
concept.intro: Prime factorization means writing a number as a product of prime numbers only. A prime number can be divided only by 1 and itself, like 2, 3, 5, and 7.
concept.keyIdea: Prime Factorization & Factor Trees. 1. Prime Number: Has exactly two factors (1 and itself, e.g. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11). 2. Split composite number into factor pairs until every branch ends in a prime. 3. Write final product using exponents in ascending order (e.g. 60 = 2² × 3 × 5)

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I want the prime factorization of 60. I start by splitting it: 60 = 6 × 10.
6 is not prime, so I break it: 6 = 2 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so I stop those branches.
10 is not prime, so I break it: 10 = 2 × 5. Both 2 and 5 are prime, so I stop.
Using exponents, I write it as 2² × 3 × 5. I check: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60. Correct.
linesEs: Quiero la descomposición en factores primos de 60. Empiezo separándolo: 60 = 6 × 10.
El 6 no es primo, así que lo separo: 6 = 2 × 3. El 2 y el 3 son primos, así que detengo esas ramas.
El 10 no es primo, así que lo separo: 10 = 2 × 5. El 2 y el 5 son primos, así que me detengo.
Ahora todos los factores son primos: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
Con exponentes, lo escribo como 2² × 3 × 5. Compruebo: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60. Correcto.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's factor 12 together. What is one way to split 12 into two factors? (You might say 3 × 4.)
Is 3 prime? Yes, so we keep it. Is 4 prime? No — what is 4 split apart? (4 = 2 × 2.)
So put the prime factors together: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. Every factor is prime, so we are done.
linesEs: Descompongamos 12 juntos. ¿De qué manera podemos separar 12 en dos factores? (Podrías decir 3 × 4.)
¿El 3 es primo? Sí, así que lo dejamos. ¿El 4 es primo? No — ¿cómo se separa el 4? (4 = 2 × 2.)
Entonces junta los factores primos: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. Todos los factores son primos, así que terminamos.

vocabulary.definition: Writing a whole number as a product of only prime numbers.
A number bigger than 1 that you can only divide by 1 and itself.
vocabulary.example: 7 has only two factors: 1 × 7. So 7 is prime.

vocabulary.definition: A number bigger than 1 that you can divide by more than just 1 and itself.
A factor of a whole number divides it evenly, with no remainder. For example, 3 is a factor of 12 because 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
A picture that splits a number into its prime numbers, step by step.
A small number that tells how many times to multiply a number by itself.

title: Synchronization Station
mission: Synchronize repeating signals. Break numbers into prime factors and predict when two cycles next meet.
investigate: List the first few multiples of each signal period.
Use prime factors to explain the first shared positive multiple.
Why is multiplying the two periods sometimes too large for the first meeting?
create: Design two repeating signals with a common meeting time. Show prime factorizations and explain exactly why that meeting time is the least common multiple.

support.prompt: What is the LCM of 3 and 5?
support.explanation: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, ... Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, ... The smallest common multiple is 15.
feedback: 3 is just one of the two numbers — it is not a multiple of 5. List the multiples of 3 and of 5 and find the first number that appears on both lists.
5 shows up when you count by 5s, but it does not show up when you count by 3s. Look for a number that is in both lists.
30 is in both lists, but it is not the smallest. Go back to the lists and stop at the first multiple they share.
hints: LCM is about MULTIPLES (counting UP by each number), not factors. You want the smallest number BOTH lists reach.
Skip count by 3s in one row and by 5s in another row, then scan for the first number that appears in both rows.
Write the 3s row: 3, 6, 9, 12, … Then start the 5s row: 5, 10, … Stop as soon as one number shows up in both rows.

support.prompt: What is the LCM of 6 and 8?
support.explanation: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, ... The smallest common multiple is 24.
feedback: 6 is a multiple of 6, but not of 8. Keep counting by 6s until you reach a number that also comes up when counting by 8s.
It looks like you added 6 + 8. The LCM does not come from adding: you need to find a number that appears in both lists of multiples.
48 is a common multiple, but a smaller number shows up on both lists first. List multiples of 8 and stop at the very first one that 6 also divides evenly.
hints: Careful: 6 + 8 is not a multiple of either number. You need a number that both 6 AND 8 divide into evenly.
List multiples of the LARGER number, 8, and check each one: is it also divisible by 6? Stop at the first hit.
Test 8: divisible by 6? No. Test 16: divisible by 6? No. Keep climbing the 8s list until a number divides evenly by 6.

support.prompt: What is the LCM of 4 and 10?
support.explanation: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ... Multiples of 10: 10, 20, ... The smallest common multiple is 20.
feedback: 2 is a common factor of the two numbers, not a common multiple. The LCM can never be smaller than 4 or 10.
10 is a multiple of 10, but not of 4. Count by 4s and check whether 10 shows up in that list.
40 = 4 × 10 is a common multiple, but multiplying the numbers doesn't always give the least one. List the multiples of 10 and stop at the first one that 4 divides.
hints: The LCM is the smallest number both 4 and 10 count into — it is often much smaller than 4 × 10 = 40.
List the multiples of 10 (the bigger number) and test each one for divisibility by 4.
Is 10 divisible by 4? 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, so no. Move up to the next multiple of 10 and run the same test.

support.prompt: What is the LCM of 2 and 7?
support.explanation: Since 2 and 7 share no common factors (they are relatively prime), LCM = 2 × 7 = 14.
feedback: 2 is a multiple of 2, but not of 7. The LCM can never be smaller than the larger of the two numbers.
That is what you get if you halved the correct amount. Instead: Since 2 and 7 share no common factors (they are relatively prime), LCM = 2 × 7 = ___.
It looks like you added 2 + 7. You find the LCM by counting multiples, not by adding the numbers.
hints: Notice that 2 and 7 are both prime — they share no common factor. That makes this a special, faster case.
List the multiples of 7 and find the first one that 2 also divides — in other words, the first EVEN multiple of 7.
Test 7: is it even? No. Move to the next multiple of 7 and check evenness again — stop at the first even one.

support.prompt: Spot Riley's Mistake — LCM of 4 and 6
steps: Problem: Find the LCM of 4 and 6.
Choose the answer: Riley added the two numbers: 4 + 6 = 10, so LCM = 10.
support.explanation: You do NOT add the numbers. The LCM is the first number that appears in BOTH multiple lists. 12 is in the multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12) and in the multiples of 6 (6, 12), so the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.
hints: Riley added 4 + 6 to get 10. Check: is 10 in both lists of multiples?
The LCM is the FIRST number that shows up in both numbers' multiple lists — look for the smallest number in both: 12.

support.prompt: Which of the following is a prime number?
support.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors: 1 and 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7, and 9 = 3 × 3, so they are all composite.
feedback: 9 splits into 3 × 3, which gives it a third factor besides 1 and 9. Keep checking each number for a hidden factor pair.
15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors besides 1 and itself. A prime number has exactly two factors — test whether any smaller number divides your choice evenly.
21 breaks apart into 3 × 7, so it has more than two factors. Look for the number that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
hints: Re-read what 'prime' means: exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Any extra factor makes a number composite.
Test each choice by dividing by small primes like 2, 3, 5, and 7. If anything divides in evenly, that number is composite.
Start with 9: since 3 × 3 = 9, it has a factor besides 1 and 9, so 9 is composite. Cross it off and test the next choice the same way.

support.prompt: What is the prime factorization of 30?
support.explanation: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. All three factors (2, 3, 5) are prime, so 2 × 3 × 5 is the prime factorization.
feedback: You started the factor tree correctly, but 15 is not prime — it still splits into 3 × 5. Keep going until every branch ends in a prime.
This is a real factor pair of 30, but 10 is composite (10 = 2 × 5). A prime factorization can only contain prime factors.
That is what you get if you stopped too early — 6 is not prime, it still breaks down into 2 x 3 — re-read what the question is asking for.
hints: A prime factorization uses ONLY prime numbers. Look at each choice: are ALL of its factors prime?
Break 30 down step by step, and keep splitting any factor that is still composite until every factor is prime.
Start with 30 = 2 × 15. Is 15 prime? No — so split 15 into two primes and collect everything you found.

support.prompt: What is the prime factorization of 18?
support.explanation: 18 = 2 × 9 = 2 × 3 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so 2 × 3 × 3 is the prime factorization.
feedback: That is what you get if you stopped too early — 9 is not prime, it still breaks down into 3 x 3 — re-read what the question is asking for.
3 is prime, but 6 is not — it still splits into 2 × 3. Keep breaking down the composite factor.
Changing the order does not fix the problem: 6 is still composite (6 = 2 × 3). Every factor in the final answer must be prime.
hints: Check every factor in each choice — numbers like 9 and 6 are composite, so they can't appear in a prime factorization.
Build a factor tree for 18: split it into two factors, then keep splitting anything composite until only primes remain.
Begin with 18 = 2 × 9. The 9 isn't prime, so break 9 into two equal prime factors and list all the primes you end with.

support.prompt: Which of these numbers is composite?
support.explanation: 27 = 3 × 9 = 3 × 3 × 3, so it has more than two factors. 23, 29, and 31 are all prime.
feedback: 23 is prime — dividing by 2, 3, or 5 always leaves a remainder. A composite number must break into smaller factors.
29 has no factor pair other than 1 × 29 — dividing by 2, 3, and 5 always leaves a remainder. A composite number has a factor pair you can actually find.
31 cannot be written as a product of two smaller whole numbers greater than 1. Test each number for a factor pair before you choose.
hints: Composite means MORE than two factors. Ask for each number: can I split it into two smaller whole numbers?
Try dividing each choice by small primes like 2, 3, and 5. A digit-sum divisible by 3 means the whole number divides by 3.
Test 23 first: try 2, 3, and 5 — none divide it evenly, so 23 is prime. Cross it off and test the other numbers the same way.

steps: Find the prime factorization of 20: Start: 20
Check each factor: 5 is prime, so that branch is done.
support.explanation: 4 is not prime because 4 = 2 × 2, so the tree needs one more split. The complete prime factorization is 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.
hints: Look at every factor in the final answer — is each one a prime number?
4 is composite because 4 = 2 × 2, so 4 still needs to be broken apart.

support.prompt: Predict the least common multiple for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: GCF(12, 18) = 6; LCM(12, 18) = 36. 12 + 18 = 6(2 + 3). A factor divides a number; a multiple is a product of the number and a whole number.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: In the prime factorization 72 = 2³ × 3², what is the sum of the exponents?
support.explanation: 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, so the exponents are 3 and 2. Their sum is 5.

core.prompt: Two buses leave the station at 8:00 AM. Bus A returns every 15 minutes and Bus B returns every 20 minutes. When is the next time both buses are at the station together?
core.explanation: LCM(15, 20) = 60 minutes. Both buses return together 60 minutes after 8:00 AM, at 9:00 AM.
feedback: Not quite. LCM(15, 20) = ___ minutes.
40 minutes works for Bus B (40 = 2 × 20), but 40 is not a multiple of 15, so Bus A has not returned yet. The moment has to work for both buses.
80 minutes is a multiple of 20 but not of 15. Extend both lists from the beginning and look for the first time they match.
hints: Both buses start together at 8:00 — they meet again after a number of minutes that both 15 and 20 divide evenly.
List each bus's return times in minutes and look for the first time that appears in both lists, then add it to 8:00 AM.
Bus A returns at 15, 30, 45, … minutes. Write Bus B's list (20, 40, …) underneath and find the first shared time, then add it to 8:00.

core.prompt: Spot Maya's Mistake — LCM of 6 and 9
steps: Problem: Find the LCM of 6 and 9.
Choose the answer: Maya saw that 9 is bigger than 6, so she wrote LCM = 9.
core.explanation: The LCM is not just the larger number. Check: 9 is in the multiples of 9, but it is NOT in the multiples of 6 (6, 12, 18...). The first number in BOTH lists is 18, so the LCM of 6 and 9 is 18.
hints: Maya picked 9 because it is the larger number. Is 9 a multiple of 6? Skip count: 6, 12, 18 — there is no 9.
The LCM must appear in BOTH multiple lists. Find the smallest number that is in the 6s AND the 9s: 18.

core.prompt: Two students found different factor trees for 60. Student A started with 2 × 30. Student B started with 6 × 10. Which statement is true?
choices: Only Student A gets the correct prime factorization
Only Student B gets the correct prime factorization
They will get different prime factorizations
Both get the same prime factorization: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5
core.explanation: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite number has exactly one prime factorization. No matter how you start the factor tree, you always end with 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
feedback: Not quite. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite number has exactly one prime factorization.
Starting with 6 × 10 is allowed, but so is starting with 2 × 30 — the opening pair does not decide who is right. Finish both trees and compare the primes at the ends.
Different starting pairs make the trees look different, but the primes at the very ends are what count. Finish both trees and list those primes before deciding.
hints: Notice the question isn't asking which START is right — it asks what happens when both finished trees are compared.
Finish BOTH trees yourself: keep splitting every branch down to primes, then compare the two final lists of prime factors.
Student A: 60 = 2 × 30, then 30 = 2 × 15, then 15 = 3 × 5. Now finish Student B's tree from 6 × 10 and compare the prime lists.

steps: Find the prime factorization of 45, using exponents: Start: 45
core.explanation: 45 = 5 × 3 × 3 has one 5 and two 3's — not two 5's. The exponent on a prime factor shows how many times that factor appears, so the correct form is 45 = 3² × 5 (the 5 has no exponent shown because it appears only once).
hints: Count how many times each prime factor actually appears in the factor tree before you write its exponent.
5 only appears once in 45 = 3 × 3 × 5, so its exponent is 1 (usually left off) — not 2.

steps: Find LCM of 8 and 12: List multiples of 8 and 12
stretch.explanation: LCM = 24 (the least common multiple is the SMALLEST shared multiple, not just any common multiple)
hints: Jaylen correctly listed the common multiples. Look at Step 5 — did he pick the smallest one?

stretch.prompt: You are making party favors. Glow sticks come in packs of 10 and bracelets come in packs of 4. What is the fewest of each you can buy so every favor has exactly one glow stick and one bracelet with none left over? Explain how the LCM solves this problem.
stretch.frame: The LCM of 10 and 4 is ___. I need to buy ___ packs of glow sticks and ___ packs of bracelets to get ___ of each. This works because ___.
stretch.explanation: Every favor uses one glow stick and one bracelet, so the totals must match and be a multiple of both 10 and 4. The LCM of 10 and 4 is 20, so you buy 2 packs of glow sticks (2 × 10 = 20) and 5 packs of bracelets (5 × 4 = 20) and finish with 20 complete favors and nothing left over.
hints: Every favor needs one of each item, so the totals must match: a number that is a multiple of 10 AND a multiple of 4.
Find LCM(10, 4) by listing multiples, then divide that LCM by 10 and by 4 to count how many packs of each to buy.
Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, … Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, … Keep both lists going until they share a number, then count packs from it.

stretch.explanation: 8 = 2 × 4, but 4 is not prime. 4 = 2 × 2, so 8 = 2 × 2 × 2. The correct prime factorization is 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3.
hints: Look at Step 4 — is every factor in the answer a prime number?
4 is not prime because 4 = 2 × 2. Marcus needed to keep breaking it down.

stretch.prompt: Choose 24, 36, or 60. Show two factor trees with different first factor pairs. Finish both trees with prime factors, then explain how you checked that both products equal your chosen number.
stretch.frame: I chose the number ___. My first factor tree starts with ___ × ___, and my second starts with ___ × ___. Both give the same prime factorization: ___. This happens because ___.
stretch.explanation: For 24, one tree starts with 2 × 12 and another with 4 × 6. Both finish with 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24. Changing the first split changes the route, but these trees give the same prime factors, including the same number of each prime.
hints: Choose 24, 36, or 60; each has at least two different nontrivial factor pairs.
Choose two different starting pairs for your number — for 36 you could start with 4 × 9 or 6 × 6 — and finish both trees to primes.
Say you pick 24: tree one starts 2 × 12, tree two starts 4 × 6. Finish both, list each tree's primes, and explain why the lists match.
